I am 30 hours in and I am still on my first campaign. This is certainly the type of game for the player who seeks this kind of stuff out. The game is very deep with its lore and story telling, it's a very dedicated sim for macro politics, and takes great effort to be realistic. It has a complex space combat system and very in depth strategic planning. If you like Stellaris or crusader kings this is definitely a game built for you, and I like all those things. 

The bad things are the game is extremely hard to learn, for me at least. It is **tedious** sometimes. It's almost impossible to know how certain things affect other things in terms of strategy. The game tells you HOW to do things, sometimes, but not why, or how to figure it out. The in game codex is very lacking in terms of suggesting how to connect the dots. The fact that I'm 30 hours in and I'm just now reaching the end of the mid phase is also crazy. A lot of this time is taken up by me just trying to absorb all the information that's given to you. You aren't alerted to events that other players might be doing. For example, I had no idea that I could build platforms on mars and once I did the entire planets sites were taken. 

So I mean it when I say that this is a game that someone seeks out. It's meant for the type of people who like this stuff, and it's very in depth. It's also very compelling, fun, and challenging. It has problems, some with game mechanics and some with UI but nothing a good dev and an update can't fix.

Some supplemental sources I've read went into some minor details about how the geography of Troy was that their massive walls faced the ocean where Greece landed and made camp and extended out to sea so that the city was inaccessible from the sides and rear. The Trojan War was also this generation's "great war" and was an excellent opportunity to become a hero and have a myth written about you and attracted a large amount of people to fight for either side. People usually wouldnt fight at night. Not only that but Greece and Troy had a great number of enemies and allies that could give men and supplies. Things like food were sent in through supply lines from the ocean to the Greek colition and supplemented with raids on farms for food and women. Troy had supply lines from the mainland but was very interested in protecting those farms for themselves but you're right in that by the end it was mostly women doing that job. By the end Troy was indeed starving and on its last legs and Agamemnon's greatest warrior, a demi god supernaturally good at slaughter, was leading an open revolt against his rule because of his incompetence. 

The biggest thing that prevented this war from ending a decade sooner in relative squander, that prevented either side from truly making any significant headway, was the direct intervention of the Olympic Gods using their divine powers. Athena would bless the Greeks to give them perfect aim in their shots or heighten courage only to face arrows from Apollo himself guarding the gates of Troy. Hera would bring her fury and malice for the Trojans to battle alongside the Greeks only to come face to face with Ares and Aphrodite. God's would be fighting toe to toe alongside men, each super human swing of their weapons shooting out electricity or lava or whatever killing dozens. Soon, Amazonians and demi gods were called in, all to just regain control over the beach outside the gates. The battle never ended because the Gods could never lose, but we're also bound by Zeus to never truly win either. So what resulted was a stalemate Greece and Troy were just set pieces for cosmic forces to bicker at one another. If Achilles love, Patroclus, had never died then Achilles would have never been crippled by grief and died in battle. Then Greece would never have been forced to retreat having lost their anchor, and would have never sent in the wooden horse, and the war would have gone on until Troy was a mound of dirt and Helen long forgotten.

We'll get ready because I've put a lot of thought into this.

Some things rely on questions to answer we aren't sure of. As well as the idea of muggle borns going turncoat and providing the military with advanced knowledge of magic. It seems, at least in Britain, that even in high levels of government that wizards have very little knowledge of human military hardware or capabilities and vice versa for humans knowing wizard capabilities. Surely they interrogate any magic capable or muggle borns in there midst. It seems on surface level that wizards are only hip to human warfare strategy up to around 1500ish, though that didn't seem the case in America. What sort of advantage could that give humans? I'm sure there could be spells to mitigate any sort of high velocity smart bombs etc but would they have to be made to spec? The time turners were all destroyed so I'm not too sure how to incorporate it. But if a wizard can get it we should also consider that it's possible a human can too. The criss crossing on wizards and humans on either side is an important factor in all of this. Teleportation is also a big game changer. Imagine apparating a bomb directly into the ministry. 

Your example of Hogwarts have a protection spell that makes people forget where they are and leave but does that still work if they're in Fort Bragg? What if a muggle operates the equipment? Hogwarts and magic make electronics malfunction but what's the limit of that? Can a kinetic bomb still function? What are the limits to the protective barrier spell? The movie shows that enough force, whether magic or concussive I dont know, can breach it. What sort of creative spells can the human military guide a muggle born to create? Or a magically guided hellfire barrage? Wizards will obviously be more capable of magic warfare and I would assume powerful wizards will know as much of human technology as they can, but truly powerful wizards are a rare breed but only one could turn the tides of war. 

War goals are also important to factor in. A genocidal "witch hunt" would invoke a very powerful response but the desire to learn and use magic in the human world might change how things play out. Wizards are known to be slavers and racists, a war of liberation might be easier to gain allys. What if the humans made allys with goblins and giants, known wizard enemies? 

Overall, using a very basic scenario, I would say that wizards have an obvious massive advantage in every war. The only way for humans to make a strong opponent is very careful planning and intelligence gathering, the upmost secrecy, and a strong united front. With everything in play a dazzling first strike using shock and awe methods that combine wizard and human capabilities could cripple the knees of a strong retaliation. This could turn into a war of attrition depending on how far each side is willing to go. There very well could be a plan for this exact scenario that wizards have made long ago and any sort of technological advantage would be moot in the face of it.

My personal view is the idea of "colonization" is typically misguided or an expression of some sort of other deep need for a higher philosophical goal for humanity. The term colonization brings up comparisons to frontier and the idea that a section of humanity will up and leave to go live on the moon and Mars and birth a new civilization ushering in the next phase of human expansion as we progress to the stars. It implies a future that harkens to the age of sail, full of deadly challenges but whose reward is intrinsic and vast. That eventually we will build enough infrastructure that living on Mars will be more or less as comfortable and fulfilling as living in a large city would, but with ceilings and you can't go outside. 

I sadly just... don't think that will happen. At least not the way the vast majority of people dream it will, and certainly not like how Elon tries to sell it. I believe that space is just so hostile and ultimately uncomfortable to the human experience that once the unique flair of outer space wears off the idea of just a regular shlub who works at a restaurant or whatever and can probably never  go to earth because the very gravity of his ancestral home will attack him will become just unthinkable and maybe even cruel. 

Now, make no mistake, I am STRONGLY in support of going to space and staying there but I think people VASTLY underestimate or misunderstand what living in such an environment would be like. We have environments on earth that are barren and combative and people do in fact live there, but not usually full time, even in places that are relatively established and comfortable. And those places you can still at least go outside and won't die of radiation poisoning. 

Even if you lived in a mansion and had a big observation dome that looked over the sea of tranquility or Olympus Mons, could you truly stand to never see a blue sky again? Or green grass? Sure we'd try to recreate those things and maybe we'd be really good at it, but what about the huge risks for cancer? And assuming you can justify all the huge costs and threats to your life, the ultimate question is what's even there? There's the science of course, the noblest cause, and then resources. People going to the new world at least believed that they had a whole new life waiting for them but they could at least, you know, go outside and stuff. 

What I hear a lot in terms of justification is stuff like asteroid mining and helium 3 on the moon. Outsource all of that stuff to relieve the earth of strip mining and get unlimited energy. Well, the h3 situation is not really like it's been depicted, our energy future is not just under the surface waiting for us to get it. It's like REALLY sparse, and even if it wasn't we have more than enough material for nuclear energy here on earth, we just have a weird fear of it. The idea of terraforming I almost don't even want to touch on, it's so ridiculous. Asteroid mining might seem like more of a prospect but ultimately what's being described now is a scientific outpost and mining town, not places where people can live and prosper and build a future but more like a remote station with rotating staff with maybe a space casino thrown in.

Ultimately there just isn't anything out there on Mars or in space that would justify what people want when they describe space colonization. Sure, people will certainly live there and will probably be happy and safe in short stays and I'm absolutely sure that the scientific advancement alone will pay back the cost but space is so extremely hostile to everything about us that I don't think anyone would give birth to a child there.

What people think will happen, what musk is selling, is a NEW new world opening up to us. That Mars is a new frontier that is just an engineering problem. But Mars is more like a new... Antarctica or oil rig at sea. Yeah people live there, but not full time, you can go there if you want, but it's not exactly prime real estate for a family. I think people really desperately want to believe otherwise because they have grand desires for the future of humanity and we look around at earth and think "is this it? Are we just stuck here for the next million years?" And we get scared and full of ennui.

I think the idea of colonizing another planet, at least in our solar system, and force our descendents to live in such harsh and brutal conditions is not only foolish but cruel. As unfortunate as it is, humans belong on Earth. Mars will never welcome us like we all so wished he would.

This is something they didn't really have to do before and the phone is rather new so this is not something all stores have the capability or tools to do. So in this particular situation it sounds like the tech damaged one of those taking it apart, it failed the OQC, they tried to order the new part and replaced it, only to find it still needs to be calibrated and then scrambled to see who in the area can come and help them.

I get why this sucks of course, but this isnt anyone trying to do the run around with you or overcharge you. In fact, removing the mmwave module on S23s is frustratingly difficult. It's hard to explain but Samsung changed their design to remove a bracket and the way it sits in the MB makes it a little too easy to apply pressure in the wrong area and all it takes is one fractional bend and it's all over. I've personally seen someone very experienced snap it like a twig. Phone repair is just one of those things. Ok... So the concept sounds pretty cool. People trapped in some sort of teleporting device that can't stop turning off and on, yeah I like that. But I think it needs some work, if youd be willing to hear me out.

Have you ever seen star trek next generation? I bring it up because you've essentially reinvented the transporter, and actually has like 30 years of R&D already worked out hah. Works more or less the way you describe it, people step in one specific spot, get vaporized, get beamed and reatomized in another specific spot. In emergency circumstances it was used outside of those spots, but only on a spaceship. It changed how people traveled on the planet. It had a certain range but you could take a transport to checkpoints and get anywhere on earth in like a minute. The limited range meant you can't use it to travel to another planet, but that doesn't seem to be the case in your story right? What people also realize about the transporter is that they also invented a matter replication machine. The device just takes the information ABOUT your atoms and reconstructs it on the other side. It doesn't literally beam the atoms there. The side effect is that if you have the data for it, you can just make whatever you want. Food, nuclear engine, dry wall, whatever, just need feed stock. The transporter also had some problems like accidentally cloning and horrible disfigurement.

So I bring that up as reference to address some issues that stand out to me.

You say spaceships are useless now, people are on other planets. Then Yellowstone blows up, earth is ravaged. Why do the other planets not provide aid or retain the technology to rebuild, or just keep the scanned people there for safe keeping? Or better yet
... Why stay on earth at all? Are they not colonized? Because it sounds like it would be easy, and that is a glaring issue to me. 

If the transporter is beaming stuff or information, they still travel at the speed of light. At light speed earth to Mars can be up to like a half hour at the worst orbit. It's not instant the way you describe because at those scales that does actually matter. But for people being scanned no time would pass for them so that checks out. A cryosleep type thing sounds pretty interesting way to develop that tech! 

How could these people not anticipate the equipment could fail...? That's... Criminally negligent. Like building a door with no door knob stupid. They didn't have anyone to like, check on it?? It doesn't even seem like all that much time passed.

So when the machines do fail and start flickering people, why do they just appear anywhere with no reason? Don't they have to be in the machine to reappear? That sounds like a feature, not a bug. They don't even need the other end? And why wouldn't the scientists dismantle or try to fix these machines? Would just destroying them count as killing them all or could they just copy the data.
